title: Al-Tabari's commentary
hookLine: the great early commentator who gathered earlier interpretations verse by verse
tomorrow: what if the best explainer of a book is the book itself?

lines: ONE STAR, FIVE STARS, SIDE BY SIDE.
cards: Scroll the reviews before you buy something and the one-star and five-star ones sit side by side. You read them all, then decide.
Al-Tabari's commentary on the Qur'an, Jami' al-Bayan, works a bit like that, and it has an odd habit. On a verse, he'll write: the people of interpretation differed about this.
Then he lists their views, one after another, each with the chain of people who passed it on. Then he says which one he thinks is right. And he leaves the others on the page.
Why keep views your own book says are weaker?

teach.b: Start with what tafsir is: explaining the Qur'an's meaning, verse by verse.
Al-Tabari gathered what the earliest generations said, companions of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, like Ibn Abbas, and the students who came after them.
Each view comes with its isnad, its chain: so-and-so heard it from so-and-so. That's your first clue. He's not only explaining; he's keeping a record.
The second clue is how he chooses. When he prefers a view, he gives reasons: the Arabic language, the flow of the passage, other reports.

teach.h: A JUDGMENT, ARGUED IN THE OPEN.
teach.b: His choice is a judgment, argued in the open, not a door slammed on the rest. And that's the answer to the puzzle.

By leaving every voice on the page, he lets a later reader check his reasoning, and even weigh it differently. He honors the people who came before him by quoting them, not by agreeing with all of them.
Here's the thing to tell a friend tonight: one of the classical commentaries is, in part, a long, careful record of disagreement. The interpreters differed, and he wrote it down.
All the voices first. Then the judgment.

how: Students of tafsir read al-Tabari's Jami' al-Bayan to see what the earliest generations said about a verse, with their chains, and how he weighed them; a teacher may assign a single verse's entry to read in full.

games.why: all the voices on the page, then a judgment argued in the open. a later reader can weigh it again.

practice: Sit still and listen for every sound around you, near and far: a fan, a car, your own breath, a voice in another room. Don't pick a favorite or push any away; just count them as they come. All the voices first.

orig.note: Arabic: Jami' al-Bayan, roughly the gathering of explanation; the short name of al-Tabari's tafsir.

carryVoice: Carry it lightly: all the voices on the page, then the judgment. Commentators, one of six.
